todays_goal: Explain what you know, not just produce an answer. Close Week 1 by strengthening academic vocabulary, reasoning, and independent work.

lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.previous_learning: Thursday showed repeated correct fraction-division work and mostly accurate decimal multiplication. One exit-ticket multiplication error showed that estimation/reasonableness checks are not yet automatic.
lessons.course_context: This closes the opening fraction/decimal fluency work before the course moves into ratios and rates, while keeping short fluency review as needed.
learning_objectives: Divide decimals by whole numbers and decimals.
Make a decimal divisor a whole number by multiplying both dividend and divisor by the same power of ten.
Estimate to check quotient magnitude and decimal placement.
Explain why equivalent scaling preserves the quotient.
lessons.why_it_matters: Decimal division is used in unit price, measurement, rates, science data, and the ratio/rate work that follows in Grade 6.

vocabulary.definition: The answer to a division problem.
The number being divided.
The number you divide by.
Equal in value even when written differently.
A close prediction used to check whether an exact answer makes sense.
The size of a number or quantity.

lessons.written_instruction: Teach decimal division conceptually. If the divisor is already whole, divide with place-value reasoning. If the divisor is decimal, multiply BOTH divisor and dividend by the same power of 10 until the divisor is whole. This creates an equivalent division problem. Estimate before or after calculating and use the estimate to detect unreasonable decimal placement.

worked_examples.title: Decimal divided by whole number
worked_examples.explanation: 72 tenths divided by 3 is 24 tenths. Estimate 6 ÷ 3 = 2, so 2.4 is reasonable.

worked_examples.title: Decimal divisor
worked_examples.explanation: Multiply both numbers by 100: 864 ÷ 27 = 32. The quotient is unchanged because both quantities were scaled by the same factor.

guided_practice.hint: Estimate first, then make the divisor whole.

guided_practice.prompt: A 12.6-meter roll is cut into 0.9-meter pieces. How many pieces?

independent_practice.prompt: A 5.4-kilogram container is divided into 0.45-kilogram packages. How many packages?
A museum charges $18.90 for 3 identical student tickets. What is one ticket?

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain why 8.64 ÷ 0.27 and 864 ÷ 27 have the same quotient.
exit_ticket.answer: Multiplying both dividend and divisor by 100 scales both by the same factor, creating an equivalent division problem with the same quotient.

exit_ticket.prompt: Estimate 3.6 ÷ 0.4, then give the exact quotient.

lessons.voice_prompt: Connect to Thursday's strong fraction division and mostly accurate decimal multiplication. Define quotient, dividend, divisor, equivalent, estimate, and magnitude. Work 7.2 ÷ 3, 8.64 ÷ 0.27, and 4.5 ÷ 0.75 completely. Explain why both dividend and divisor scale together. Ask a verbal check using 6.3 ÷ 0.9. Use hints before answers and protect exit-ticket answers.
lessons.teacher_notes: Move forward to decimal division. If exit is 4/5+ and explanation is sound, begin ratios next week with decimal fluency warmups.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.lesson_title: Precise topic, central idea, and objective summary
lessons.previous_learning: Thursday comprehension was solid, but the topic was too vague and the objective summary omitted important causes/details.
lessons.course_context: The opening reading unit builds precise evidence-based reading before longer novel and research work.
learning_objectives: Name a precise topic.
State a complete central idea.
Explain how details support the central idea.
Write a 2-3 sentence objective summary without opinion.
lessons.why_it_matters: Precise topic and summary skills support science, history, research, and analytical writing.

vocabulary.definition: The increase in size of a material as it warms.
To become smaller.
A designed gap or flexible connection that allows parts of a structure to move.
Internal force created when a material is pushed, pulled, bent, or prevented from moving.
The main point an author communicates about a topic.
A short account of the most important ideas without personal opinion.

lessons.written_instruction: Read the teacher-created article 'Why Bridges Need Room to Move' twice. First read for meaning; second read for evidence. Topic must be a specific subject phrase, not a vague word. Central idea must be a complete sentence. Summary should include the phenomenon, the problem, and the engineering response without opinion.

worked_examples.title: Topic vs central idea
worked_examples.problem: Article about sleep and brain function
worked_examples.solution: Topic: sleep and brain function. Central idea: Regular sleep supports attention, memory, and health.
worked_examples.explanation: A topic names the subject; a central idea states the author's main point about it.

worked_examples.title: Objective summary check
worked_examples.solution: Use factual explanation without 'obviously', 'I think', or personal judgment.
worked_examples.explanation: Objective summaries report the text rather than evaluate it.

guided_practice.prompt: State the central idea in one complete sentence.

independent_practice.prompt: Explain what happens to bridge materials when they warm.
Define stress from context.
Explain why blocked expansion can cause damage.
Give two engineering solutions.
Write a 2-3 sentence objective summary.

exit_ticket.prompt: What makes a topic precise rather than vague?
exit_ticket.answer: It names the specific subject of the text rather than using a broad word such as difference or things.

exit_ticket.prompt: What three parts should today's objective summary include?
exit_ticket.answer: The temperature-driven movement, the damage/stress problem when movement is blocked, and the engineering response that allows controlled movement.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach precise topic vs central idea vs objective summary. Connect to Thursday's vague topic and incomplete summary. Do not reveal the article's central idea before Atticus reads. Ask what the author most wants the reader to understand and which details support it.
lessons.teacher_notes: Keep reading level at Grade 6; focus on precision, not easier text.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.lesson_title: Explain why with evidence and reasoning
lessons.previous_learning: Across Week 1, Atticus's ideas are often stronger than the completeness and precision of his written responses.
lessons.course_context: The opening writing unit builds complete evidence-based paragraphs before multi-paragraph explanatory and argument writing.
learning_objectives: Write an 8-10 sentence explanatory paragraph.
Use at least two specific facts from a source.
Explain why each fact matters.
Revise sentence clarity and punctuation.
lessons.why_it_matters: Evidence plus reasoning is required across literature, science, history, and later essays.

vocabulary.definition: Writing that teaches how or why something happens.
The sentence that states the main explanation.
A fact or detail that supports an explanation.
The explanation of why evidence supports the main idea.
A word or phrase that helps ideas connect.
To improve ideas, organization, wording, or sentence clarity.

lessons.written_instruction: Use the bridge reading as evidence. Plan main explanation, evidence 1 + why it matters, evidence 2 + why it matters, and conclusion. Draft 8-10 complete sentences, then revise one sentence at a time for clarity and conventions.

worked_examples.title: Evidence only
worked_examples.explanation: Reasoning is still needed to show why that fact matters to bridge design.

worked_examples.title: Evidence plus reasoning
worked_examples.solution: Steel expands when heated, so long bridge sections need room to move; otherwise stress can build and damage the structure.
worked_examples.explanation: The reasoning links evidence to the design choice.

guided_practice.prompt: State the main explanation in one sentence.
Choose two article facts and explain why each matters.

independent_practice.prompt: Write 8-10 sentences answering: Why do engineers design bridges with expansion joints or other ways to allow movement?

exit_ticket.prompt: Underline one evidence sentence and circle the reasoning that follows it.
exit_ticket.answer: Student should identify a source fact and the explanation connecting it to the claim.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach evidence vs reasoning explicitly. Model one weak and one strong example. Ask Atticus to state his explanation and two pieces of evidence verbally before he writes. Do not compose the final paragraph for him.
lessons.teacher_notes: Emphasize sentence completeness and explicit reasoning.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.previous_learning: Thursday showed strong light-source -> object -> eye reasoning, but transparent/translucent/opaque vocabulary was applied inconsistently.
lessons.course_context: The Light & Matter unit develops models of how light travels and interacts with materials before later energy units.
learning_objectives: Distinguish transparent, translucent, and opaque using evidence.
Explain that light can transmit without preserving a clear image.
Use transmission and scattering observations to justify classification.
lessons.why_it_matters: Scientific classification depends on observable evidence and precise vocabulary.

vocabulary.definition: To let light pass through.
To redirect light in many directions.
Transmits most visible light with little scattering, allowing a clear image.
Transmits some visible light but scatters it, so images are blurry or unclear.
Does not transmit visible light through the material.
To take in light energy rather than transmit or reflect it.

lessons.written_instruction: Separate two questions: does light get through, and does detailed image information remain clear? Use flashlight-to-wall observations to classify actual household materials. Materials vary, so observations control the label.

worked_examples.title: Transparent
worked_examples.solution: Light passes and image details remain clear.

worked_examples.title: Translucent
worked_examples.solution: Some light passes but image details are lost.

worked_examples.title: Opaque
worked_examples.solution: Visible light does not pass through.
worked_examples.explanation: No transmitted light behind the material.

guided_practice.prompt: Predict which material will transmit most clearly and explain why.

independent_practice.prompt: Run the flashlight-to-wall material lab and complete the table.
Draw a ray model showing transmitted/scattered/reflected/absorbed light.
Write a CER explaining how a material can transmit light without giving a clear image.

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain translucent vs opaque in your own words.
exit_ticket.answer: Translucent materials transmit some light but scatter it; opaque materials do not transmit visible light through them.

exit_ticket.prompt: Does reflecting some light automatically make a material opaque? Explain.
exit_ticket.answer: No. Many materials both reflect and transmit some light; opacity depends on whether visible light is transmitted through the material.

lessons.voice_prompt: Connect to Thursday's strong light-path model and vocabulary confusion. Define transmit, scatter, transparent, translucent, opaque, absorb. Stress that light can pass without a clear image. Guide prediction and evidence-based classification; do not force household samples into labels contrary to observations.
lessons.teacher_notes: Vocabulary precision is the focus; core light-path concept is already strong.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.previous_learning: Thursday showed strong mountain -> difficult travel -> separate city-state reasoning. Sea benefits and culturally connected vs politically unified need reinforcement.
lessons.course_context: The Ancient Greece unit moves from geography to the polis before Athens, Sparta, democracy, war, philosophy, and the wider Greek world.
learning_objectives: Define polis/city-state.
Explain how mountains supported political independence.
Explain how the sea supported trade, travel, fishing, and exchange.
Distinguish cultural connection from political unity.
lessons.why_it_matters: This explains why Greek communities could share culture while developing different governments and rivalries.

vocabulary.definition: An independent Greek city-state and its surrounding territory.
A city and nearby territory functioning as an independent political unit.
Governing itself rather than being ruled by one larger central government.
Sharing language, beliefs, customs, stories, or practices even without one government.
A sheltered place where ships can anchor safely.
Exchange of goods, resources, or services.

lessons.written_instruction: Read 'From Mountains and Harbors to the Polis.' Use cause/effect chains and the glossary. Correct Thursday's seawater misconception: the sea's major benefits were transportation, trade, fishing, communication, and exchange, not drinking water.

worked_examples.title: Cause/effect chain
worked_examples.explanation: Geographic barriers made regular land connection difficult, supporting local independence.

worked_examples.title: Culture vs politics
worked_examples.problem: Can two poleis share language and gods but have separate governments?
worked_examples.explanation: Cultural connection does not require political unification.

guided_practice.prompt: Explain one sea benefit and one mountain effect.

independent_practice.prompt: Define polis.
Give three ways the sea helped Greek communities.
Explain why trade mattered with limited farmland.
Explain culturally connected vs politically unified.
Explain how mountains and sea together shaped the Greek world.

lessons.voice_prompt: Define polis, city-state, politically independent, culturally connected, harbor, trade. Correct seawater misconception gently. Ask Atticus to explain the geography -> travel -> communities -> political development chain and the culture/politics distinction before independent work.
lessons.teacher_notes: Keep causal reasoning central rather than memorizing names alone.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.previous_learning: Thursday showed mostly correct ne...pas structure, with errors in elision before vowels and je/tu verb endings.
lessons.course_context: The opening French unit consolidates present tense, negation, questions, and conversational accuracy before high-frequency irregular verbs.
learning_objectives: Use regular -ER endings accurately.
Use ne...pas correctly.
Use n' before vowel sounds.
Answer short spoken questions in complete French sentences.
lessons.why_it_matters: Accurate high-frequency sentence patterns make later conversation and reading much easier.

vocabulary.definition: A word such as je, tu, il, elle, nous, vous, ils, elles that tells who does the action.
The part of a regular verb left after removing -er.
Letters added to the stem to match the subject.
To change a verb form to match the subject.
A form that makes a sentence negative, such as ne...pas.
Dropping a vowel before another vowel sound; ne becomes n'.

lessons.written_instruction: Review -ER endings: je -e, tu -es, il/elle -e, nous -ons, vous -ez, ils/elles -ent. Put ne/n' before the conjugated verb and pas after it. Use n' before a vowel sound: elle n'écoute pas. Contrast je joue with tu joues.

worked_examples.title: Negation
worked_examples.solution: Je ne regarde pas la télévision.
worked_examples.explanation: ne goes before the conjugated verb and pas after it.

worked_examples.title: Elision
worked_examples.explanation: ne becomes n' before a vowel sound.

guided_practice.prompt: Say three negative -ER sentences aloud with the tutor.

independent_practice.prompt: Complete Friday French written practice: negation, conjugation, and full-sentence answers.

exit_ticket.answer: Before a following vowel sound or silent h.

exit_ticket.prompt: Conjugate jouer for je and tu.

lessons.voice_prompt: Review -ER endings and teach elision explicitly. Contrast je joue / tu joues. Conduct at least four short spoken questions and require full-sentence responses. Correct gently and let Atticus repeat the repaired form.
lessons.teacher_notes: Continuing French; do not restart as beginner French.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.lesson_title: Rule-based programs vs machine learning; generalization
lessons.previous_learning: Thursday Scratch and Teachable Machine builds were completed successfully, but the written comparison and exit-ticket explanation were unfinished.
lessons.course_context: The opening CS/AI unit distinguishes explicit algorithms from learned models before loops, variables, data, and deeper AI literacy.
learning_objectives: Distinguish a programmer-written rule from a learned classifier.
Define training data, label, confidence, classifier, generalization, and debugging.
Test an image classifier under new conditions.
Explain why high confidence can still be wrong.
lessons.why_it_matters: Understanding what an AI model learned - and what it did not learn - is fundamental AI literacy.

vocabulary.definition: A program that follows explicit instructions written by a programmer.
A method in which a system learns patterns from examples instead of receiving every decision rule directly.
Examples used to teach a machine-learning model.
The correct category name attached to a training example.
A model that assigns an input to one of several categories.
The model's estimate of how strongly an input matches a class; not a guarantee of correctness.
To work correctly on new examples that were not in the training set.
Finding and fixing a problem in a program or system.

lessons.written_instruction: Compare Thursday's Scratch IF/ELSE program with Teachable Machine. Scratch follows an explicit threshold rule written by the programmer. Teachable Machine learns visual patterns from labeled examples. Then run an online variation experiment: test familiar classes under new angles/backgrounds/lighting, add varied training examples to the weakest class, retrain, and compare.

worked_examples.title: Rule-based
worked_examples.problem: IF temperature > 75 THEN say warm ELSE say not above 75.
worked_examples.explanation: The computer follows it exactly rather than learning it from examples.

worked_examples.title: Machine learning
worked_examples.solution: The model learns patterns from the examples.
worked_examples.explanation: The decision boundary is learned from data rather than written explicitly for every image.

worked_examples.title: Confidence is not certainty
worked_examples.problem: Model predicts cup at 98% for an unfamiliar object.
worked_examples.explanation: The score reflects the model's comparison among known classes, not proof about the real-world object.

guided_practice.prompt: Explain who wrote the Scratch rule and what Teachable Machine used instead.

independent_practice.prompt: Run the Teachable Machine generalization experiment using household objects only.
Record new-condition results, retraining changes, and unfamiliar-object behavior.

exit_ticket.prompt: Who wrote the Scratch decision rule?
What did Teachable Machine use to learn categories?

exit_ticket.answer: Rule-based systems follow explicit programmer-written rules; machine-learning systems learn patterns from training data.

exit_ticket.prompt: Why can a classifier be highly confident and still wrong?
exit_ticket.answer: Limited or biased training data and unfamiliar inputs can produce a strong internal score that does not match the real-world object.
Perform correctly on new examples or conditions not seen exactly during training.
Finding, understanding, and fixing a problem in a program or system.

lessons.voice_prompt: Connect directly to Thursday's completed Scratch and Teachable Machine builds. Define rule-based program, ML, training data, label, classifier, confidence, generalize, debugging. Explain confidence is not certainty. Guide the online variation experiment without using faces or personal information.
lessons.teacher_notes: Practical building is strong; Friday closes the conceptual comparison and tests generalization.

lessons.subject: art_design
lessons.previous_learning: Prior FWCD art work showed strong engagement and craftsmanship. This homeschool course begins with information design and visual explanation.
lessons.course_context: Art/Design combines drawing, visual communication, critique, and portfolio work throughout the year.
learning_objectives: Use visual hierarchy intentionally.
Create one clear central diagram/visual.
Use annotations and a caption to teach an idea accurately.
Produce a portfolio-ready one-page explainer.
lessons.why_it_matters: Visual communication is used in science, engineering, design, presentations, and everyday media.

vocabulary.definition: The order in which a viewer notices information.
A noticeable difference that helps important elements stand out.
A simple image or mark that represents an idea.
A short label or note added to explain part of a visual.
The arrangement of elements on a page.
Brief text that explains an image or diagram.

lessons.written_instruction: Choose one Week 1 concept and create a one-page visual explainer on separate blank paper. Include a clear title, one main diagram/visual, at least three useful annotations, deliberate hierarchy/contrast, and a 2-3 sentence accurate caption.

worked_examples.title: Hierarchy
worked_examples.problem: Everything on the page is the same size.
worked_examples.solution: Make the title largest, central visual second, and labels smaller.
worked_examples.explanation: Size and contrast guide the viewer through information.

guided_practice.prompt: Decide what the viewer should notice first, second, and third.

independent_practice.prompt: Create the final visual explainer on a separate blank sheet.

exit_ticket.prompt: In one sentence, explain one design choice you made to improve clarity.
exit_ticket.answer: Answers vary; should reference hierarchy, contrast, layout, labeling, or another deliberate design choice.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach visual hierarchy, contrast, symbol, annotation, composition, and caption. Help Atticus plan rather than decorate. Require title, central visual, at least three labels, hierarchy, and an accurate 2-3 sentence caption. Do not design the final piece for him.
